Bonytail chub Gila elegans in the lower Colorado River basin typically achieve an ultimate total length of 62 centimeters [Li = 62 centimeters], a size that distinguishes this species from its sympatric cyprinid relatives. Field surveys conducted in the early 2000s documented that gravid females measuring 51.8 cm in total length carry an impressive fecundity of approximately 103 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 103 eggs per spawning event] with around 377 spawning events per year [F_R_i = around 377 spawning events per year] when the annual average water temperature hovers near 21 °C [T = 21 °C], equivalent to an ultimate reproductive rate of approximately 103 eggs per day . This daily reproductive output reflects the high spawning frequency during the spring and early summer months, when monsoonal flows trigger upstream migrations and subsequent gamete release. The species is iteroparous, with individuals participating in multiple spawning events over the course of a single reproductive season. Such a strategy is consistent with other large-bodied cyprinids endemic to the warm, turbid waters of the Colorado River, where episodic flooding creates windows of favorable conditions for egg and larval survival. Indeed, the maximum annual reproductive rate observed in this population underscores the species capacity to rapidly colonize newly inundated floodplain habitats when conditions permit.

At the onset of exogenous feeding, newly hatched prolarvae weigh approximately 0.0028 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0028 grams], representing the average wet weight at hatch measured under controlled laboratory conditions. This diminutive mass reflects the relatively small, demersal eggs produced by this species, which are adhesive and settle onto cobble substrate after broadcast spawning. In stark contrast, fully grown adults attain a wet weight of roughly 3,300 grams [Wwi = roughly 3,300 grams], a figure derived from applying the length-weight conversion 0.00813 multiplied by total length raised to the 3.13 power. The enormous disparity between natal and adult body mass—spanning six orders of magnitude—underscores the remarkable growth trajectory that bonytail chub undergo during their ontogeny. Following hatch, the yolk-sac larva remains endotrophic for a brief period, relying on internal yolk reserves before the mouth opens and the trophic switch to exogenous feeding occurs. These early life stages are particularly vulnerable to predation by non-native species such as striped bass and sunfish, which have contributed to the precipitous decline of wild populations throughout the 20th century.

Embryonic development proceeds rapidly at the thermal regime typical of spring spawns, with the average age at hatch estimated at approximately 9 days [ab = approximately 9 days] when eggs are incubated at 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C]. This value represents the arithmetic mean of hatching times recorded across two separate laboratory trials, the first yielding 170 hours and the second 269 hours, normalized to a per-day quotient. During this interval, the chorionate embryo progresses through cleavage, blastula, and gastrula stages before chorionase secretion triggers eclosion. After emergence, the prolarvae remain largely inactive, clinging to substrate or vegetation until yolk sac absorption is complete, at which point the exotrophic transition begins. Water temperature exerts a profound influence on developmental rate, and deviations from the optimal 16.5 °C regime can either accelerate or delay hatching by several days. Field observations suggest that spawning events closely track rising spring temperatures, with egg deposition occurring when the river warms to approximately 15–18 °C, thereby synchronizing hatching with peak zooplankton abundance.

Evaluating the species longevity reveals that bonytail chub can persist for up to 1,825 days [am = up to 1,825 days] under natural conditions, a lifespan of roughly five years when water temperatures average 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This maximum recorded longevity was established through otolith annuli analysis of wild-caught specimens collected during the 1990s, before the most severe population crashes occurred. Compared to other Colorado River cyprinids such as the razorback sucker Xyrauchen texanus, which can exceed 40 years, the bonytail lifespan is modest, suggesting a faster pace of life with earlier maturation and higher reproductive investment. The thermal regime experienced throughout the year—broadly fluctuating between winter lows near 8 °C and summer highs exceeding 28 °C—likely constrains metabolic rate and somatic growth, contributing to this relatively compressed lifespan. In captive hatchery settings, individuals have occasionally survived beyond seven years, though such instances are rare and may reflect the absence of predation and disease pressures found in the wild. Conservation hatcheries have therefore prioritized early reproduction over extended longevity in their broodstock management protocols.

Sexual maturation in bonytail chub occurs after approximately 730 days after hatching [tp = approximately 730 days after hatching], a time since birth at puberty that reflects the species adaptation to a variable desert river environment at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. Puberty is reached when the water temperature averages near 13 °C [T = near 13 °C], coinciding with the cooler transitional period between winter and early spring. At this stage, vitellogenesis onset is initiated in females, while males undergo spermatogenesis activation, marking the commencement of gonadal recrudescence. This relatively delayed maturation—spanning two full years—is an intermediate strategy among cyprinids; some introduced species like common carp mature within one year, while the humpback chub Gila cypha, a close congener, is also reported to reach puberty at approximately the same age. Following maturation, individuals participate in their first spawning event during the subsequent spring migration, thereby completing the life cycle from hatch to first reproduction in roughly three years. The timing of puberty appears sensitive to local thermal conditions, as populations occupying warmer tailwater reaches below dams have been observed to mature several months earlier than those in unregulated segments.
